teams.outlook: Josh Allen remains the offense's floor and ceiling under Joe Brady, with rushing volume (his stickiest predictor) keeping him a locked top-3 QB in this 6-pt format; James Cook enters a contract year with bell-cow volume but TD equity (16 last year) is a regression risk, while the WR room behind him stays target-share diffuse enough to cap any single non-Allen weapon as a low-end WR2/3.

Mike McDaniel's scheme still leans on pace and motion, but Tua Tagovailoa's injury pattern (multiple concussions) discounts his floor every week; Tyreek Hill's TPRR and explosive-play role keep him fantasy-viable but age (32) puts him on the back half of the WR aging curve, and De'Von Achane's receiving role gives him a real PPR floor even if early-down work is shared.

New staff continuity questions persist after last year's upheaval; Justin Fields' rushing volume (if he's the starter) is the swing factor for his fantasy value far more than his passing efficiency, and Garrett Wilson's target share should stay elite regardless of QB, making him a buy even amid offensive uncertainty.

Josh McDaniels/Mike Vrabel-era continuity around Drake Maye enters year two with expanded weapons; Maye's dual-threat rushing plus a full offseason as starter make him a sneaky top-10 QB target in a 6-pt league, and TreVeyon Henderson's receiving-down role gives him standalone PPR value even in a run-funnel offense.

Todd Monken's offense keeps Lamar Jackson as the QB1 archetype for this format — elite rushing volume plus 6-pt TD passing is nearly unmatched ceiling — while Derrick Henry's age (32) and 350+ touch workload last year put him squarely in cliff territory even though goal-line role stays intact.

Zac Taylor's pass-heavy, high-pace offense keeps Joe Burrow's efficiency elite when healthy, but the calf/turf-toe injury history is a real games-missed discount; Ja'Marr Chase remains a top-3 WR lock on target share and TD equity alone, immune to scheme noise.

Arthur Smith's run-funnel, tight-end-heavy scheme caps whoever plays QB (Fields/Wilson competition) and pushes value toward the ground game; Najee Harris's departure (if applicable) or Jaylen Warren's role change is the swing variable for RB volume — target the back who wins clear early-down/goal-line work over any passing-game complement.

QB competition remains the swing engine for the whole offense; whoever wins the job inherits a run-first identity that suppresses passing volume, meaning receivers here should be priced as low-floor dart throws until a starter is confirmed and the pecking order stabilizes.

Nick Caley's new-ish offensive command still funnels through C.J. Stroud's efficiency, and Stroud's turnover-prone stretches (concussion/uncertainty history) warrant modest discounting; Nico Collins remains a locked-in target-share stud, while Joe Mixon's age/injury profile makes him a touchdown-dependent RB2 rather than a bell-cow lock.

Shane Steichen's up-tempo, QB-friendly system with Daniel Jones or Anthony Richardson at the helm (rushing floor either way) keeps this offense fantasy-relevant; Jonathan Taylor's touch volume and goal-line role make him a top-5 non-PPR RB as long as the O-line holds, but his age (26-27) puts him near the start of the RB decline window — sell-high candidate at peak trade value.

Liam Coen's arrival (McVay-tree install) is the single biggest scheme change for Trevor Lawrence's fantasy outlook — expect more play-action, RPOs, and a cleaner progression read that should boost efficiency and touchdown rate; Travis Etienne's receiving role and Brian Thomas Jr.'s year-2 target-share expansion (post-rookie breakout) make both prime buys under the new system.

Brian Callahan enters year two with more continuity and a healthier o-line outlook; Cam Ward's rookie-year rushing ability and a full offseason as the unquestioned starter give him sneaky QB streaming value, while Tony Pollard's role is touchdown-capped in a run-funnel, low-scoring context.

Sean Payton's aggressive, RPO-infused scheme keeps Bo Nix's efficiency trending up in year two — the classic Payton QB2-to-QB1 leap profile — and Courtland Sutton's contested-catch role stays a TD-equity strength in this non-PPR-leaning brief, though PPR here still rewards volume; watch RJ Harvey's touches as the likely lead back in a friendly scheme.

Andy Reid's system stays pass-heavy and Patrick Mahomes remains a high-floor top-8 QB even amid recent efficiency dips, but the post-Kelce tight end void and diffuse WR room (Rashee Rice's role/health, Xavier Worthy's big-play-only profile) mean no single Chiefs pass-catcher should be drafted as a locked top-12 asset — target-share uncertainty caps ceilings across the board.

Jim Harbaugh/Greg Roman's run-heavy, physical identity with Justin Herbert caps QB upside somewhat but keeps Omarion Hampton (touch volume, goal-line role as a rookie-year breakout candidate) as one of the best non-PPR RB profiles in the league — draft capital plus clear early-down role is the exact breakout template.

Chip Kelly's tempo-based install (new OC) is the wildcard for Geno Smith/rookie QB competition and Ashton Jeanty's touches; Jeanty's draft capital (top-10 pick) and clear bell-cow usage make him a strong buy even in an offense whose passing details remain unresolved heading into camp — lingering camp questions here are a real red flag for confident WR projections.

Brian Schottenheimer's first year as OC/HC brings scheme uncertainty for Dak Prescott, but Prescott's efficiency history and the league's 6-pt passing TD bonus keep him a high-floor QB1; CeeDee Lamb's target share stays elite regardless of playcaller, making him scheme-proof at the top of WR rankings.

New-ish coaching staff (per camp reports) with a QB competition (Jaxson Dart's rookie developmental path vs veteran) means backfield touches should be prioritized over unproven passing-game roles; Tyrone Tracy's receiving-down role gives him standalone value if he wins the early-down job outright.

Kevin Patullo's continuity from the Shane Steichen-built system keeps Jalen Hurts' rushing floor (goal-line TD equity is the stickiest part of his profile) fully intact even amid efficiency questions; Saquon Barkley's post-2,000-yard workload age-27 season is a mild cliff-risk flag despite elite talent — buy the role, temper the ceiling expectations from last year's outlier.

Kliff Kingsbury's aggressive, deep-shot scheme should amplify Jayden Daniels' rushing+passing dual-threat ceiling in year two (the exact profile the meta favors for early QB investment), while Terry McLaurin's contested-catch, TD-equity role stays a locked WR2/3 floor regardless of scheme tweaks.

Ben Johnson's Lions-tree install is the single most important variable in fantasy for 2026 — improved play-design, motion, and red-zone efficiency should push Caleb Williams into a legitimate year-2 leap (ESPN's own headline flags this explicitly), and D'Andre Swift/Roschon Johnson's roles should get a real bump in scoring efficiency from better O-line and scheme support.

John Morton/Sam Barrington-led offense (post-Ben Johnson/Aaron Glenn departures) keeps Jared Goff's efficiency dependent on Amon-Ra St. Brown's elite target share, but coaching continuity questions in Detroit make this offense's floor slightly less certain than last year's projections assume; Jahmyr Gibbs remains a locked non-PPR/PPR dual-threat stud as the clear lead back.

Matt LaFleur's offense returns largely intact and ESPN's own framing ('Pack primed for a playoff run') signals positive market momentum; Jordan Love's efficiency plus Josh Jacobs' bell-cow, goal-line-heavy role (a clean non-PPR volume profile) make Jacobs a strong buy at current cost, with Jayden Reed's TD-equity role as the WR2 to target.

ESPN's own headline flags QB play as the persistent question mark here — whoever starts (veteran competition) caps the passing game's ceiling, meaning Justin Jefferson's target share stays elite but his efficiency/TD output is QB-play-dependent, and Jamal Adams' arrival is a defensive-side move with no direct offensive fantasy consequence.

Zac Robinson's second year installing the Rams-tree scheme should smooth out Michael Penix Jr.'s progression as full-time starter, and Bijan Robinson's expanding receiving role under this scheme makes him a top-3 non-PPR/PPR RB with true bell-cow volume.

Dave Canales' scheme continues to feature designed QB runs for Bryce Young, giving him a modest rushing floor that helps his fantasy value more than his still-shaky efficiency, while Chuba Hubbard's clear-cut early-down role stays a solid RB2 floor in a run-funnel offense.

Kellen Moore's new offensive install brings a more RPO/play-action-heavy structure, but the QB situation remains unresolved enough that no Saints skill-position player should be drafted with confidence until camp clarifies the starter and Alvin Kamara's touch share amid his age-30 season.

Josh Grizzard/Liam Coen-departure continuity questions aside, Baker Mayfield's efficiency and Mike Evans' contested-catch TD equity remain steady; the Vita Vea trade request is a defensive/locker-room story with no direct offensive fantasy value but signals possible roster instability worth monitoring.

With Jacoby Brissett's deal done and fully entrenched in the playbook, the Cardinals' passing offense gets a stabilizing, if low-ceiling, veteran presence while Kyler Murray's health/roster status remains the swing variable; James Conner's touchdown-dependent, age-30 profile is a fade candidate at cost given his workload history.

Sean McVay's offense remains one of the league's most efficient scheme-driven environments for Matthew Stafford, and Kyren Williams' clear bell-cow, goal-line-heavy role (classic non-PPR gold) stays a top-10 RB lock as long as he's healthy; Puka Nacua's route-running/target-share floor is scheme-proof at the top of the WR pool.

Kyle Shanahan's continued personal involvement with Brock Purdy (per camp reports) signals no QB controversy, keeping Purdy's efficient, play-action-driven passing floor intact; Christian McCaffrey's age-30, injury-history profile (Achilles/calf issues) is a real discount factor even amid a full recovery narrative — buy the role, not the age.

Klint Kubiak's play-caller continuity into year two with Sam Darnold gives the passing game a stabilizing baseline, and Kenneth Walker III's clear-cut lead-back role (assuming health) keeps him a solid RB2 floor with upside if the offensive line camp reports trend positive.

season_storylines: Ben Johnson's arrival in Chicago is the marquee scheme story of the offseason — a Lions-tree install (motion, RPOs, red-zone design) that directly targets Caleb Williams' year-2 leap and lifts the whole skill-position group's efficiency ceiling.

Liam Coen's move to Jacksonville imports the McVay-tree passing structure that fueled LA's efficiency boom, pointing to real touchdown-rate and target-share gains for Trevor Lawrence, Brian Thomas Jr., and Travis Etienne.

The 6-pt passing-TD/-2 INT scoring in this league keeps elite, low-INT pocket passers (Burrow, Prescott, Mahomes) priced a full round higher than 4-pt consensus while doubling the tax on turnover-prone arms — draft QB efficiency, not just volume.

QB competitions remain unresolved in Cleveland, Pittsburgh, New Orleans, and arguably Las Vegas/New York (Giants) heading into camp — treat every skill player on those offenses as a hold-until-clarity dart rather than a locked-in asset.

Multiple age-30+ workhorse backs (Derrick Henry, Alvin Kamara, James Conner) carry real cliff risk after heavy multi-year touch totals — the RB age curve says sell or fade at current ADP even where role looks stable on paper.

Second-year QBs with rushing floors (Caleb Williams, Jayden Daniels, Bo Nix) are the format's best value tier — the meta-trend of early-round mobile QBs paying off (2022-2025) plus new/continuing scheme installs around them raises their ceiling further.

Rookie-year bell-cow backs with clear draft capital and role (Ashton Jeanty in Las Vegas, Omarion Hampton in LA) fit the strongest predictive template — R1 draft capital plus early bell-cow usage — for immediate RB1 production regardless of offensive uncertainty elsewhere.

Kansas City's post-Kelce tight end void and diffuse WR competition (Rice health, Worthy's big-play-only profile) mean no single Chiefs pass-catcher is a safe top-12 lock this year despite Mahomes' continued floor.
Defensive locker-room instability stories (Vita Vea's trade request in Tampa) are worth monitoring for roster-composition ripple effects but carry no direct offensive fantasy consequence this season.

Camp-report signals (ESPN's own team-by-team intel pieces) on O-line health and QB competition should be weighted heavily in the final two weeks before your draft — several teams' fantasy ceilings (NYG, CLE, LV, NO) are still genuinely unresolved.
